source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. X (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio primi capituli: Verbum Domini, quod factum est ad Joel filium Phatuel.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: The word of the Lord, that came to Joel the son of Phatuel.

paras.t: Præmittit Joel libro suo breve proœmium, quod finitur ibi, Audite. Itaque ait : Verbum Domini, id est sermo propheticus, quod factum est ad Joel filium Phatuel, id est per angelicam subministrationem inspiratum, et interna sive externa locutione divinitus dictum Joeli filio Phatuelis : qui Phatuel creditur fuisse propheta, juxta regulam Hebræorum, dicentium omnes illos fuisse prophetas, qui in titulis Prophetarum ponuntur ut patres eorum. Vel potest intelligi de increato Verbo Patris æterni Unigenito Dei, ut sit sensus : Verbum Domini, de quo scriptum est, In principio erat Verbum, est illud quod factum est ad Joel, id est Joeli locutum ac manifestatum per illustrationem propheticam. Porro propheticæ illuminationes, ut frequentius, factæ sunt per locutionem internam atque imaginariam visionem, sive in somno, sive in vigilia per abstractionem a sensu exteriori. Interdum tamen factæ sunt per exteriorem apparitionem ac sensibilem allocutionem, ut patet de Daniele. Aliquando etiam factæ sunt per solam intellectualem illustrationem : quod tamen, secundum Thomam, conditionem propheticæ cognitionis aliquo modo transcendit, sicut in David.
paras.en: Joel prefixes to his book a short proem, which ends where he says, *Hear*. So he says: [[1:1|The word of the Lord|Verbum Domini]], that is, the prophetic discourse, [[1:1|that came to Joel, the son of Phatuel|quod factum est ad Joel filium Phatuel]]: that is, inspired through the ministry of angels, and spoken by God to Joel the son of Phatuel by inward or outward speech. This Phatuel is believed to have been a prophet, according to the rule of the Hebrews, who say that all those were prophets who are set down in the titles of the Prophets as their fathers. Or it can be understood of the uncreated Word of the eternal Father, the Only-begotten of God, so that the sense is: the Word of the Lord, of whom it is written, [[John 1:1|In the beginning was the Word|In principio erat Verbum]], is that which came to Joel, that is, was spoken and made manifest to Joel through prophetic enlightenment. Now prophetic illuminations were for the most part made through inward speech and imaginary vision [that is, a vision formed in the imagination, as distinct from bodily sight or pure understanding], whether in sleep or, while awake, through withdrawal from the outward senses. Sometimes, however, they were made through an outward apparition and a speaking perceptible to the senses, as is plain in the case of Daniel[[Dan 9:21||]][[Dan 9:22||]][[Dan 10:9||]]. And sometimes they were made through intellectual enlightenment alone: which, however, according to Thomas, in some way goes beyond the condition of prophetic knowledge, as in David.

paras.t: Consequenter Propheta ex magnitudine dicendorum, auditores reddit attentos. Provocans ergo ad dicendorum advertentiam diligentem : Audite, inquit, hoc quod dicam, o senes, id est, auribus cordis et corporis verba mea advertite ; et auribus percipite, omnes habitatores terræ, id est, ceteri omnes seu populares. Per senes vero accipi possunt non solum antiquiores ætate, sed judices ordinarii, qui septuaginta senioribus a Moyse constitutis successerunt. Senes autem qui experientia, maturitate atque scientia eminent, honorandi sunt, et merito prænominandi, quemadmodum in Levitico dicitur : Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis. Hoc ergo pensate, si factum est istud quod dicam, id est, an simile aliquid contigit, in diebus vestris, aut in diebus patrum vestrorum. Tanquam dicat : Nec in diebus vestris, nec tempore parentum vestrorum tale quid accidit. Per patres autem, non solum proximos genitores, sed et avos atavosque significat, secundum Hieronymum. An tamen omnes illos usque ad Abraham, non est certum. Sumitur autem hoc loco si, pro non, sicut in Psalmo : Si introiero in tabernaculum domus meæ, si ascendero in lectum strati mei ; et in Isaia : Juravit Dominus, Si dimittetur vobis iniquitas hæc, donec moriamini.
paras.en: Next the Prophet, from the greatness of what he is to say, makes his hearers attentive. Calling them, then, to give careful heed to what he will say: [[1:2|Hear|Audite]], he says, [[1:2|this|hoc]] that I shall say, [[1:2|ye old men|o senes]]: that is, attend to my words with the ears of heart and body; [[1:2|and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land|et auribus percipite, omnes habitatores terræ]], that is, all the rest, or the common people. By *old men* may be understood not only those older in age, but the ordinary judges, who succeeded the seventy elders appointed by Moses[[Num 11:16||]][[Num 11:24||]]. And old men who excel in experience, maturity and knowledge are to be honoured, and rightly named first, as is said in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:32|Rise up before the hoary head, and honour the person of the aged man|Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis]]. Weigh this, then: [[1:2|did this ever happen|si factum est istud]] that I shall tell, that is, has anything like it befallen, [[1:2|in your days, or in the days of your fathers|in diebus vestris, aut in diebus patrum vestrorum]]? As if to say: Neither in your days nor in the time of your forefathers did any such thing happen. By *fathers* he means not only the nearest parents but also grandfathers and ancestors, according to Jerome. Whether, however, all of them back to Abraham, is not certain. Here *si* [*if*] is taken for *not*, as in the Psalm: [[Ps 131:3|If I shall enter into the tabernacle of my house: if I shall go up into the bed wherein I lie|Si introiero in tabernaculum domus meæ, si ascendero in lectum strati mei]] [that is, I will not enter, I will not go up; the Douay-Rheims keeps the Latin *if*]; and in Isaias: The Lord swore, [[Is 22:14|Surely this iniquity shall not be forgiven you till you die|Si dimittetur vobis iniquitas hæc, donec moriamini]] [here the Douay-Rheims renders the *si* as a denial].

paras.t: Super hoc, id est de ista materia tam miranda, filiis vestris narrate quæ auditis a me, ut pater filiis notam faciat veritatem. Pater enim debet filio educationem, correctionem et instructionem. Et filii vestri filiis suis eadem narrent, et filii eorum generationi alteræ, id est, posteris suis hæc recitent, ut nulla oblivione deleantur. Vel, Generationi alteræ, id est genti alienæ. Quod impletum est per Apostolos, qui gentilibus ad fidem conversis hæc nuntiaverunt, et usque in præsens a Christianis memoriter recoluntur. Simile huic exhortationi est illud in Psalmo : Quanta mandavit patribus nostris, nota facere ea filiis suis, ut cognoscat generatio altera ; filii qui nascentur et exsurgent, et narrabunt filiis suis. Quo enim fuerint opera Dei mirabiliora, majora aut rariora, eo sunt amplius recolenda.
paras.en: [[1:3|Tell ye of this|Super hoc]], that is, of this matter so wonderful, [[1:3|to your children|filiis vestris narrate]] what you hear from me, so that [[Is 38:19|the father shall make the truth known to the children|pater filiis notam faciat veritatem]]. For a father owes his son upbringing, correction and instruction. [[1:3|and let your children tell their children|Et filii vestri filiis suis]] the same things, [[1:3|and their children to another generation|et filii eorum generationi alteræ]]: that is, let them recount these things to their descendants, so that they may be blotted out by no forgetting. Or, *to another generation*, that is, to a foreign nation. This was fulfilled through the Apostles, who announced these things to the Gentiles converted to the faith, and to this day they are kept in memory by Christians. Like this exhortation is that in the Psalm: [[Ps 77:5|How great things he commanded our fathers, that they should make the same known to their children|Quanta mandavit patribus nostris, nota facere ea filiis suis]]: [[Ps 77:6|That another generation might know them. The children that should be born and should rise up, and declare them to their children|ut cognoscat generatio altera ; filii qui nascentur et exsurgent, et narrabunt filiis suis]]. For the more wonderful, great or rare the works of God have been, the more they are to be recalled.

paras.t: Deinde ponitur narratio, incipitque tractatus. Residuum erucæ comedit locusta, et residuum locustæ comedit bruchus, et residuum bruchi comedit rubigo. Eruca est vermis qui in oleribus maxime invenitur ac nascitur. Bruchus autem et locusta sunt unius speciei. Nam bruchus est proles locustæ : qui quum fuerit alatus, cœperitque volare, vocatur locusta, quæ est animal breve ac parvum. Rubigo vero vocatur corruptio seu vitium segetum, quando scilicet teneræ fruges nocivo rore aut vento percussæ, faciunt pauca aut nulla grana, ita quod culmi seu stipulæ et spicæ in ruborem quemdam vertuntur.
paras.en: Then the narrative is set down, and the treatise begins. [[1:4|That which the palmerworm hath left, the locust hath eaten: and that which the locust hath left, the bruchus hath eaten: and that which the bruchus hath left, the mildew hath destroyed|Residuum erucæ comedit locusta, et residuum locustæ comedit bruchus, et residuum bruchi comedit rubigo]] [literally, *the mildew hath eaten*]. The *eruca* [palmerworm] is a worm that is found and bred chiefly among garden herbs. The bruchus and the locust are of one species: for the bruchus is the offspring of the locust, which, when it has grown wings and begun to fly, is called a locust; it is a short, small creature. *Rubigo* [mildew; literally *rust*, from its reddish colour] is the name for a blight or disease of the crops, when, that is, the tender grain, struck by a harmful dew or wind, yields few grains or none, so that the stalks or straw and the ears turn a kind of red.

paras.t: Hunc locum doctores diversimode exponunt. Judæi autem, ut refert Hieronymus, dicunt hæc litteraliter accidisse, ita quod tempore Joelis vel circiter, venerunt innumerabiles locustæ in terram promissionis, quæ non solum fruges, sed insuper vinearum ac arborum ramos et cortices consumpserunt ; quod vero locustis residuum mansit, bruchus subsequens devoravit. Unde et aliqui expositores catholici, sequentes in hoc dicta Hebræorum, dicunt quod in terram duodecim tribuum venerunt successive hæ quatuor pestes seu plagæ, ita quod terræ nascentia primo ab erucis corrosa sunt ; secundo a locustis, vorantibus pro magna parte quod superfuit erucis ; tertio a bruchis, comedentibus partim residua locustarum ; quarto a rubigine, quæ totum consumpsit quod reperit. Unde et Glossa dicit quia historialiter potuit esse, quod hæc omnia simul venerunt tempore Eliæ et Achab, quando facta est fames et siccitas annis tribus et mensibus sex. Alii referunt ad famem factam tempore Elisei et Joram filii Achab, durantem septem annis : de qua Eliseus prænunciavit mulieri Sunamiti, consulens ut pergeret in terram Philistinorum, ut legitur quarto Regum. Sic ergo Joel dicit, quod huic negotio non accidit simile, quoniam unaquæque plagarum istarum per se satis molesta est, sed quum omnes simul eveniunt, durissima pestis est.
paras.en: The doctors expound this place in different ways. The Jews, as Jerome relates, say that these things happened literally: that about the time of Joel countless locusts came into the land of promise, which consumed not only the crops but also the branches and bark of the vines and trees; and what was left by the locusts, the bruchus that followed devoured. Hence some Catholic expositors too, following in this the sayings of the Hebrews, say that these four pests or plagues came one after another into the land of the twelve tribes, so that what grew from the earth was gnawed first by palmerworms; secondly by locusts, devouring for the most part what the palmerworms had left; thirdly by the bruchus, eating part of what the locusts left; fourthly by the mildew, which consumed all it found. Hence the Gloss too says that historically it may have been that all these came together in the time of Elias and Achab, when there was famine and drought for three years and six months[[3 Kings 17:1||]][[3 Kings 18:1||]][[Jas 5:17||]]. Others refer it to the famine that came in the time of Eliseus and Joram the son of Achab, which lasted seven years: of which Eliseus forewarned the Sunamite woman, advising her to go into the land of the Philistines, as we read in the fourth book of Kings[[4 Kings 6:25||]][[4 Kings 8:1||]][[4 Kings 8:2||]]. So then Joel says that nothing like this affair ever happened, since each of these plagues by itself is troublesome enough, but when all come at once it is a most grievous pestilence.

paras.t: Hieronymus autem videtur hæc reprobare, quia (ut dicit) si hæc ad litteram accidissent, liber Regum vel Paralipomenon non hæc tacuissent, sicut de duplici fame præfata liber Regum non tacet. Cui objiciunt alii, quod non omnia quæ contingunt, scribuntur, quemadmodum de terræ motu facto tempore Oziæ regis Juda, quum voluit thurificare, prædicti libri nil referunt, sed Amos et Zacharias inde commemorant.
paras.en: Jerome, however, seems to reject this, because (as he says) if these things had happened literally, the book of Kings or of Paralipomenon would not have passed them over in silence, just as the book of Kings is not silent about the two famines mentioned. Against him others object that not everything that happens is written down: thus of the earthquake that took place in the time of Ozias king of Juda, when he sought to offer incense[[2 Par 26:16||]], the said books relate nothing, but Amos and Zacharias make mention of it[[Amos 1:1||]][[Zach 14:5||]].

paras.t: Aliqui igitur dicunt quod negotium istud fuit res gesta, seu veritas, et figura, ita quod per prædictorum animalium atque rubiginis plagam, præfigurabantur quatuor magnæ plagæ Judæorum, a quatuor regnis, videlicet ab Assyriis, Chaldæis, Græcis et Romanis, eis illatæ. Quidam autem Assyrios et Chaldæos pro eodem computant regno, quoniam ab eodem mundi climate contra Israelitas venerunt ; et Persas ac Medos annumerant regnis quæ vastarunt Judæos. Dicit quippe Hieronymus, quod Hebræi per erucam intelligunt Assyrios et Chaldæos (Assyrii enim regnum decem tribuum destruxerunt ; Chaldæi vero, regnum Juda); per locustas autem, Persas ac Medos, qui Chaldæorum regno destructo, habuerunt Judæos captivos. Per bruchum vero intelligunt Macedones seu Græcos, scilicet reges successores Alexandri Magni, præsertim Antiochum Nobilem, qui tanquam bruchus cum suis sedens in Judæa, pene omnia devoravit ; per rubiginem autem, Romanum imperium, a quo maxime atque finaliter sunt dejecti, et de terra sua totaliter pulsi. Verumtamen, quoniam reges Persarum ac Medorum non fuerunt Judæis multum molesti, sed quidam eorum fuerunt ipsis plurimum gratiosi, sicut Cyrus qui dedit ipsis licentiam redeundi in propria, et Assuerus; idcirco non computavit regnum Medorum atque Persarum inter prædicta regna Judæos vastantia, sed regnum Assyriorum distinguit a regno Chaldæorum. Hæc sunt quatuor cornua, et quatuor venti, de quibus (ut infra patebit) loquitur Zacharias.
paras.en: Some, then, say that this affair was both a thing done, or a truth [of history], and a figure: so that by the plague of the said creatures and of the mildew were prefigured four great plagues brought upon the Jews by four kingdoms, namely by the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Greeks and Romans. Some, however, count the Assyrians and Chaldeans as one kingdom, since they came against the Israelites from the same region of the world; and they number the Persians and Medes among the kingdoms that laid waste the Jews. For Jerome says that the Hebrews understand by the palmerworm the Assyrians and Chaldeans (for the Assyrians destroyed the kingdom of the ten tribes[[4 Kings 17:3||]], and the Chaldeans the kingdom of Juda[[4 Kings 25:1||]]); by the locusts, the Persians and Medes, who, when the kingdom of the Chaldeans was destroyed, held the Jews captive. By the bruchus they understand the Macedonians or Greeks, that is, the kings who succeeded Alexander the Great, above all Antiochus the Illustrious [*Nobilis*: Antiochus Epiphanes], who, settled like a bruchus with his men in Judea, devoured almost everything[[1 Mach 1:1||]] [the margin gives 1 Mach. i et seq., ii, iii, vi]; and by the mildew, the Roman empire, by which they were most of all and finally cast down, and wholly driven out of their land. Yet since the kings of the Persians and Medes were not very troublesome to the Jews, but some of them were most gracious to them, as Cyrus, who gave them leave to return to their own land[[1 Esd 1:2||]], and Assuerus[[Esth 8:1||]][[Esth 9:1||]], he therefore did not count the kingdom of the Medes and Persians among the said kingdoms that laid waste the Jews, but distinguishes the kingdom of the Assyrians from that of the Chaldeans. These are the four horns and the four winds of which (as will appear below) Zacharias speaks[[Zach 1:18||]][[Zach 6:5||]].

paras.t: Denique, quidam eorum qui asserunt litteraliter gestum quod de eruca, locusta, brucho, ærugine scriptum est, aiunt plagas has non uno anno vel tempore, sed diversis annis sibi invicem succedentibus accidisse. Sed secundum hoc, non apparet quomodo unum genus bestiarum istarum vorasset quod alteri residuum fuit, præsertim quum singulis annis terræ nascentia oriantur, et deposita recondantur : nisi forte dicantur hæ bestiæ habitacula hominum introisse.
paras.en: Lastly, some of those who maintain that what is written of the palmerworm, locust, bruchus and rust [*ærugo*, that is, the mildew] was literally done, say that these plagues happened not in one year or at one time, but in different years following one after another. But on this view it does not appear how one kind of these creatures could have devoured what another had left, especially since every year the fruits of the earth spring up anew, and what is gathered is stored away: unless perhaps these creatures are said to have entered men's dwellings.

paras.t: Itaque, sicut jam tactum est, secundum Hieronymum, iste est sensus litteræ hujus : Residuum erucæ, id est populum Juda seu Israel non vastatum ab Assyriis et Chaldæis, vastabant Persæ ac Medi ; et quem illi non vastarunt, oppresserunt Græci successores Alexandri, de quibus agitur in libro Machabæorum ; Judæos vero non oppressos a Græcis, oppresserunt Romani. Huic autem expositioni quidam objiciunt, quia de corrosione terræ nascentium ab eruca, locusta, etc., fit hic tam evidens mentio, quod non videtur aliquo modo esse parabola. Sed quidquid sit de veritate, argumentum istud nullius valoris est : quoniam in Scripturis divinis multa parabolice denuntiantur, et homines nomine bestiarum aliarumque rerum significantur, ubi fit multo apertior atque prolixior mentio de nominibus bestiarum inanimatarumque rerum, quam hic. Quemadmodum apud Isaiam legitur : Habitabit lupus cum agno, et pardus cum hœdo accubabit ; vitulus et leo et ovis simul morabuntur, et puer parvulus minabit eos. Vitulus et ursus pascentur, simul requiescent catuli eorum ; et leo quasi bos comedet paleas. Omnia autem hæc et quædam sequentia, exponuntur ad litteram, non de animalium horum domesticatione, sed de hominum diversarum conditionum pacifica in Ecclesia cohabitatione, secundum omnes doctores catholicos. Et multa similia in Scripturis habentur, præsertim (ut reor) in Isaia, cujus liber difficilior comprobatur.
paras.en: So, as has already been touched on, according to Jerome this is the sense of this text: [[1:4|That which the palmerworm hath left|Residuum erucæ]], that is, the people of Juda or Israel not laid waste by the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the Persians and Medes laid waste; and those whom they did not lay waste, the Greeks, the successors of Alexander, oppressed, of whom the book of Machabees treats; and the Jews not oppressed by the Greeks, the Romans oppressed. Against this exposition some object that the gnawing of the fruits of the earth by the palmerworm, locust, etc., is mentioned here so plainly that it does not seem in any way to be a parable. But whatever be the truth of the matter, that argument is of no value: for in the divine Scriptures many things are declared in parables, and men are signified by the names of beasts and other things, where the names of beasts and inanimate things are mentioned much more openly and at greater length than here. As we read in Isaias: [[Is 11:6|The wolf shall dwell with the lamb: and the leopard shall lie down with the kid: the calf and the lion, and the sheep shall abide together, and a little child shall lead them|Habitabit lupus cum agno, et pardus cum hœdo accubabit ; vitulus et leo et ovis simul morabuntur, et puer parvulus minabit eos]]. [[Is 11:7|The calf and the bear shall feed: their young ones shall rest together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox|Vitulus et ursus pascentur, simul requiescent catuli eorum ; et leo quasi bos comedet paleas]]. All these things and some that follow are expounded literally, according to all Catholic doctors, not of the taming of these animals but of the peaceful dwelling together in the Church of men of different conditions. And many like things are found in the Scriptures, above all (I think) in Isaias, whose book proves the more difficult.

paras.t: Expergiscimini, ebrii, id est, vos qui estis vitiis et passionibus sic involuti, vel potu sic repleti, quod a recto mentis statu prolapsi estis, nec rationis judicium imitamini, neque pericula vobis imminentia ponderatis, evigilate redeundo ad cor, et a torpore ac negligentia vestra cessate, et flete, vitia vestra lacrimis pœnitentiæ redimendo ; et ululate propter tribulationes instantes, omnes qui bibitis vinum in dulcedine, id est carnali delectatione, non necessitatem naturæ, sed gustus voluptatem quærentes ; quoniam periit ab ore vestro, id est, in proximo est ut vina ac cetera carnis delectabilia auferantur a vobis, sicut mox subditur. Loquitur autem Propheta de futuro per modum præteriti, propter certitudinem veritatis. Prophetica quippe cognitio, est quædam imago atque impressio notitiæ mentis divinæ, in qua omnia quasi præsentialiter lucent et agnoscuntur, tamque infallibiliter sciuntur, sicut ea quæ fuerunt certissimum est fuisse.
paras.en: [[1:5|Awake, ye that are drunk|Expergiscimini, ebrii]]: that is, you who are so wrapped up in vices and passions, or so filled with drink, that you have fallen from the right state of mind, and neither follow the judgement of reason nor weigh the dangers hanging over you, wake up by returning to your heart, and cease from your torpor and negligence; [[1:5|and weep|et flete]], redeeming your vices with tears of penance; [[1:5|and mourn|et ululate]] [*ululate*, howl] for the tribulations at hand, [[1:5|all ye that take delight in drinking sweet wine|omnes qui bibitis vinum in dulcedine]] [literally, *who drink wine in sweetness*], that is, with carnal delight, seeking not the need of nature but the pleasure of taste; [[1:5|for it is cut off from your mouth|quoniam periit ab ore vestro]]: that is, it is close at hand that wine and the other delights of the flesh will be taken from you, as is added just after. Now the Prophet speaks of the future in the manner of the past, because of the certainty of the truth. For prophetic knowledge is a kind of image and imprint of the knowledge of the divine mind, in which all things shine and are known as if present, and are known as infallibly as it is most certain that what has been, has been.

paras.t: Gens enim ascendet, id est veniet, super terram meam, id est Judæam : quæ dicitur specialiter terra Dei, quia ad divinum cultum electa, et populo Dei a Deo promissa atque collata; fortis et innumerabilis, secundum apparentiam : non tamen fuit simpliciter innumerabilis, quia in numero, mensura et pondere constituta sunt omnia; vel, Innumerabilis, ob multitudinem suam. Potestque gens ista intelligi exercitus Chaldæorum, vel etiam Assyriorum, Græcorum, ac Romanorum. Dentes ejus, ut dentes leonis, id est, omnia crudeliter dilaniabit; et molares ejus, videlicet dentes majores, utpote potestas principum populi hujus atque sævitia, sunt ut catuli leonis, ita quod cum omni tyrannide populum Judæorum vastabit : bona terræ consumet, urbes demolietur, et nec ætati parcet, nec sexui.
paras.en: [[1:6|For a nation come up|Gens enim ascendet]] [Denis reads *ascendet*, shall come up], that is, shall come, [[1:6|upon my land|super terram meam]], that is, Judea, which is called in a special way the land of God, because it was chosen for divine worship, and promised and given by God to the people of God; [[1:6|strong, and without number|fortis et innumerabilis]], in appearance: yet it was not simply without number, since all things are set in number, measure and weight[[Wis 11:21||]]; or, *without number* because of its multitude. And this nation can be understood as the army of the Chaldeans, or also of the Assyrians, Greeks and Romans. [[1:6|his teeth are like the teeth of a lion|Dentes ejus, ut dentes leonis]], that is, he will tear all things cruelly to pieces; [[1:6|and his cheek teeth|et molares ejus]], that is, the larger teeth, namely the power and fierceness of the princes of this people, are [[1:6|as of a lion's whelp|ut catuli leonis]]: so that he will lay waste the people of the Jews with all tyranny: he will consume the goods of the land, demolish the cities, and spare neither age nor sex.

paras.t: Posuit vineam meam in desertum, id est, Synagogam occidit vel transtulit, in solitudinemque redegit. De qua vinea dictum est in Isaia : Vinea Domini exercituum, domus Israel est; et in Jeremia, Ego te plantavi vineam electam. Et ficum meam decorticavit, id est, populum meum quem quasi fructum dulcem et filios procreavi et alui, minoravit, multos eorum occidendo. Nudans vineam istam, id est, bona ejus tollens ab ea, spoliavit eam bonis mobilibus ac immobilibus, et projecit in captivitatem vel mortem. Albi facti sunt rami ejus, id est, filii ejus arefacti sunt et occisi. Vel sensus est, quod hostes destruxerunt vineas et arbores fructiferas in Judæa. Quod certum est contigisse Nabuchodonosor tempore, postmodum quoque sub Antiocho Nobili, et tempore Titi et Vespasiani.
paras.en: [[1:7|He hath laid my vineyard waste|Posuit vineam meam in desertum]] [literally, *hath made my vineyard a desert*], that is, he has slain or carried away the Synagogue, and reduced it to a wilderness. Of this vineyard it is said in Isaias: [[Is 5:7|the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel|Vinea Domini exercituum, domus Israel est]]; and in Jeremias: [[Jer 2:21|I planted thee a chosen vineyard|Ego te plantavi vineam electam]]. [[1:7|and hath pilled off the bark of my fig tree|Et ficum meam decorticavit]], that is, he has diminished my people, whom I begot and nourished as a sweet fruit and as sons, by slaying many of them. Laying bare this vineyard, that is, taking its goods from it, [[1:7|he hath stripped it bare|spoliavit eam]] of goods movable and immovable, [[1:7|and cast it away|et projecit]] into captivity or death. [[1:7|the branches thereof are made white|Albi facti sunt rami ejus]], that is, its sons have been dried up and slain. Or the sense is that the enemies destroyed the vineyards and fruit trees in Judea. This certainly happened in the time of Nabuchodonosor, and afterwards also under Antiochus the Illustrious, and in the time of Titus and Vespasian.

paras.t: Quæritur quomodo injusti Judæi, de quibus jam dixit, Expergiscimini, ebrii, appellentur ficus et vinea Dei. Et respondendum, quod eo modo quo Christus in Evangelio vocat reprobos Judæos, filios regni : Filii, inquit, regni ejicientur in tenebras exteriores. Vocantur itaque ficus et vinea Dei, quoniam Deus multa beneficia concessit ac præbuit eis, specialiter vocans eos ad cultum et gratiam suam, et quoniam Patriarcharum ac Prophetarum filii erant.
paras.en: It is asked how the unjust Jews, of whom he has just said, [[1:5|Awake, ye that are drunk|Expergiscimini, ebrii]], can be called the fig tree and the vineyard of God. And the answer is: in the way in which Christ in the Gospel calls the reprobate Jews *children of the kingdom*: [[Matt 8:12|the children|Filii]], he says, [[Matt 8:12|of the kingdom shall be cast out into the exterior darkness|regni ejicientur in tenebras exteriores]]. So they are called the fig tree and vineyard of God, since God granted and bestowed many benefits on them, calling them in a special way to his worship and grace, and since they were the sons of the Patriarchs and Prophets.

paras.t: Quum ergo tanta tibi, o popule Judæorum, instet calamitas, Plange tua peccata, ut misericordiam consequaris : plange autem toto affectu, et abundanter ac perseveranter, quasi virgo accincta sacco super virum pubertatis suæ, id est, quemadmodum plorat virgo juvencula desponsata, propter mortem sponsi sui qui moritur antequam ejus cupitis fruatur amplexibus. Vir autem et sponsus Synagogæ fuit Deus omnipotens, qui in Patriarchis et in datione legis desponsavit sibi Synagogam.
paras.en: Since then so great a calamity threatens thee, O people of the Jews, [[1:8|Lament|Plange]] thy sins, that thou mayest obtain mercy; and lament with all thy heart, abundantly and perseveringly, [[1:8|like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth|quasi virgo accincta sacco super virum pubertatis suæ]]: that is, as a young betrothed maiden weeps for the death of her bridegroom, who dies before she can enjoy the embraces she longs for. Now the husband and bridegroom of the Synagogue was almighty God, who betrothed the Synagogue to himself in the Patriarchs and in the giving of the Law.

paras.t: Quamdiu autem Synagoga per idololatriam et alia gravia scelera non recessit a Deo, erat sponsa et virgo mentis integritate, in cognitione, amore et cultu veri Dei. Tempore autem Joelis meretrix facta propter multiplicia scelera, monetur super virum pubertatis suæ, id est de cœlestis Sponsi amissione, cordialiter flere.
paras.en: As long as the Synagogue did not depart from God through idolatry and other grave crimes, she was a bride and a virgin in integrity of mind, in the knowledge, love and worship of the true God. But in the time of Joel, having become a harlot through her many crimes, she is warned to weep from the heart [[1:8|for the husband of her youth|super virum pubertatis suæ]], that is, over the loss of the heavenly Bridegroom.

paras.t: Periit sacrificium et libatio de domo Domini : id est, terræ nascentibus et ceteris possessionibus devoratis ab hostibus præinductis, vel bestiolis prænominatis, defecit in templo Jerusalem sacrificium, quod erat de materia solida, scilicet tritico, hordeo, carne; et libatio, id est immolatio de materia liquida, utpote vino et oleo. Deficiente enim causa, deficit et effectus. Et luxerunt sacerdotes ministri Domini, id est, vehementer contristati sunt, et planxerunt, tum propter cultus divini cessationem, tum propter cessationem immolationum earum rerum de quibus sustentabantur. Eratque luctus hic bonus, quantum ad primum, quia ex zelo divini honoris processit; et etiam quantum ad secundum, si planctus propter defectum oblationis victualium erat, in quantum victualia debite ordinantur ad spirituale bonum animæ et ad obsequium Dei. Si autem sacerdotes respexerunt ad proprium commodum, privatumque bonum, non erat illorum planctus meritorius et acceptus. Porro sacerdotes specialiter dicti sunt ministri Dei, quia ad altaris obsequium deputati, atque pro primogenitis filiorum Israel Domino ministrantes in templo. Hinc enim in libro Numerorum Moyses dixit Levitis : Num parum vobis est, quod separavit vos Dominus a populo, et junxit sibi, ut serviretis ei in cultu tabernaculi, et staretis coram eo, et coram frequentia populi? Ezechias quoque secundo libro Paralipomenon ait Levitis : Filii mei, nolite negligere : vos enim elegit Dominus, ut stetis coram eo, et ministretis ei, colatisque eum, et cremetis ei incensum.
paras.en: [[1:9|Sacrifice and libation is cut off from the house of the Lord|Periit sacrificium et libatio de domo Domini]]: that is, since what grows from the earth and the other possessions have been devoured by the enemies spoken of, or by the little creatures named above, there has failed in the temple of Jerusalem the sacrifice, which was of solid matter, namely wheat, barley and flesh; and the libation, that is, the offering of liquid matter, such as wine and oil. For when the cause fails, the effect fails too. [[1:9|the priests, the Lord's ministers, have mourned|Et luxerunt sacerdotes ministri Domini]]: that is, they were grievously saddened and lamented, both for the ceasing of divine worship and for the ceasing of the offerings of those things by which they were sustained. And this mourning was good as to the first, since it came from zeal for God's honour; and also as to the second, if the lament for the lack of an offering of victuals was in so far as victuals are duly ordered to the spiritual good of the soul and to the service of God. But if the priests looked to their own advantage and private good, their lament was not meritorious or acceptable. Further, the priests are in a special way called ministers of God, since they were appointed to the service of the altar, and ministered to the Lord in the temple in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel. Hence in the book of Numbers Moses said to the Levites: [[Num 16:9|Is it a small thing unto you, that the God of Israel hath spared you from all the people, and joined you to himself, that you should serve him in the service of the tabernacle, and should stand before the congregation of the people|Num parum vobis est, quod separavit vos Dominus a populo, et junxit sibi, ut serviretis ei in cultu tabernaculi, et staretis coram eo, et coram frequentia populi?]]? Ezechias too, in the second book of Paralipomenon, says to the Levites: [[2 Par 29:11|My sons, be not negligent: the Lord hath chosen you to stand before him, and to minister to him, and to worship him, and to burn incense to him|Filii mei, nolite negligere : vos enim elegit Dominus, ut stetis coram eo, et ministretis ei, colatisque eum, et cremetis ei incensum]].

paras.t: Depopulata est regio, id est, regnum Juda sic demolitum est, ut et homines, et animantia, ac terræ nascentia sint destructa. Luxit humus, id est, terra Judææ privata est solitis fructibus : sicque metaphorice luxit, quemadmodum fertur ridere quum abundat germinibus, fructu floreque vernans. Ideo subditur : quoniam devastatum, id est, ab adversariis devoratum est triticum : per quod alia blada dantur intelligi. Confusum est vinum, elanguit oleum. Sicut de humo seu terra dictum est, quod metaphorice fertur planxisse propter carentiam fructuum ; sic confusum est vinum, id est ablatum, ita quod consuetum effectum habere non potuit exhilarando bibentes, et prædictos vinolentos suo defectu ostendit confusos, dum sperato desolati sunt potu. Pariformiter elanguit oleum, id est, defecit et alios ostendit infirmos, qui oleo deficiente pariter contabuerunt.
paras.en: [[1:10|The country is destroyed|Depopulata est regio]]: that is, the kingdom of Juda has been so demolished that men, beasts and the fruits of the earth are destroyed. [[1:10|the ground hath mourned|Luxit humus]]: that is, the land of Judea has been deprived of its accustomed fruits; and so it has mourned metaphorically, just as it is said to laugh when it abounds in shoots, blooming with fruit and flower. Therefore it is added: [[1:10|for the corn is wasted|quoniam devastatum]] (that is, devoured by the adversaries) [[1:10|the corn|est triticum]], by which the other grains are given to be understood. [[1:10|the wine is confounded, the oil hath languished|Confusum est vinum, elanguit oleum]]. As it was said of the ground or earth that it is metaphorically said to have lamented for lack of fruits, so [[1:10|the wine is confounded|confusum est vinum]], that is, taken away, so that it could not have its accustomed effect of gladdening those who drink it, and by its failing it showed the drunkards spoken of to be confounded, when they were left desolate of the drink they hoped for. In like manner [[1:10|the oil hath languished|elanguit oleum]], that is, it failed, and showed others to be weak, who wasted away alike when the oil failed.

paras.t: Confusi sunt agricolæ, id est spe sua frustrati, dum fructu agrorum quos coluerunt, privati sunt, ululaverunt vinitores super frumento, vino et hordeo, id est de horum fructuum ablatione seu deprædatione; quia periit messis agri, id est, congregatio fructuum præfatorum in agris nascentium sublata est eis tunc, quando præ manibus habuerunt fruges messionis. Molestissimum siquidem est, tunc frugibus terræ spoliari, quando ad maturitatem usque deductæ sunt, custoditæ atque speratæ.
paras.en: [[1:11|The husbandmen are ashamed|Confusi sunt agricolæ]], that is, frustrated in their hope, being deprived of the fruit of the fields they tilled; [[1:11|the vinedressers have howled for the wheat|ululaverunt vinitores super frumento]], the wine [[1:11|and for the barley|et hordeo]] [Denis's text has *vino*, wine, which the Vulgate lacks], that is, for the taking away or plundering of these fruits; [[1:11|because the harvest of the field is perished|quia periit messis agri]]: that is, the gathering of the said fruits growing in the fields was taken from them just when they had the harvest crops in hand. For it is most grievous to be robbed of the fruits of the earth just when they have been brought to ripeness, guarded and hoped for.

paras.t: Vinea confusa est, et ficus elanguit : id est, vineæ et ficeta fructibus suis sunt destituta per erucam, locustam, bruchum, rubiginem; vel hostibus tradita, puta Chaldæis, Assyriis, vel Romanis. Malogranatum, et palma, et malum, id est arbores sic vocatæ, et omnia ligna agri, id est reliquæ arbores infructuosæ sive fructiferæ, aruerunt, id est, marcida facta sunt plagis præmemoratis : cujus signum est, quia confusum, id est ablatum, est gaudium a filiis hominum, id est a Judæis, qui de prædictis bonis terræ gaudere solebant. Porro per filios hominum, hoc loco ad litteram intelliguntur Judæi, quibus loquebatur Joel. Qui et specialiter dicuntur filii hominum, puta eorum qui humane rationabiliterque vixerunt, hoc est Patriarcharum, Prophetarum, ac justorum veteris Testamenti. Denique malogranatum, cujus cortici in Canticis comparantur genæ Sponsæ, est arbor medicinalis (secundum Glossam), cujus poma sunt rubea, ad edendum amara. Et dicitur malogranatum, quoniam fructus ejus multa continet grana.
paras.en: [[1:12|The vineyard is confounded, and the fig tree hath languished|Vinea confusa est, et ficus elanguit]]: that is, the vineyards and fig orchards have been stripped of their fruits by the palmerworm, locust, bruchus and mildew; or handed over to the enemies, say the Chaldeans, Assyrians or Romans. [[1:12|the pomegranate tree, and the palm tree, and the apple tree|Malogranatum, et palma, et malum]], that is, the trees so called, [[1:12|and all the trees of the field|et omnia ligna agri]], that is, the remaining trees, fruitless or fruitful, [[1:12|are withered|aruerunt]], that is, have become withered by the plagues mentioned; and the sign of this is, [[1:12|because joy is withdrawn|quia confusum]], that is, taken away, [[1:12|from the children of men|est gaudium a filiis hominum]], that is, from the Jews, who used to rejoice in the said goods of the land. Further, by *the children of men* are here literally understood the Jews, to whom Joel was speaking. They are also specially called children of men, that is, of those who lived in a humane and reasonable way: of the Patriarchs, the Prophets and the just of the Old Testament. Lastly, the pomegranate, to whose rind the cheeks of the Bride are compared in the Canticles[[Cant 6:6||]], is a medicinal tree (according to the Gloss), whose fruits are red, and bitter to eat. And it is called *malogranatum* [*grained apple*] because its fruit contains many grains.

paras.t: Accingite vos sacco et cilicio, et plangite, sacerdotes; ululate, ministri altaris. Eumdem sensum aliis verbis resumit, ut fortius excitet audientes. Sacerdotum autem præcipue est, propria ac subditorum deflere peccata, et Deum populo reconciliare, quum sint inter Deum ac populum mediatores, offerendo preces et hostias populi Deo, gratiamque Dei populo reportantes. Quum autem ex negligentia sacerdotum provenit populi culpa, maxime congruit sacerdotibus flere pro populi reconciliatione : quia et Dominus dixit ad Moysen, quod filii Aaron portarent peccata filiorum Israel. Ingredimini templum, vel propriam domum ad orandum : sicut ait Salvator, Tu autem quum oraveris, intra cubiculum tuum, et ora Patrem tuum in absconso; cubate, id est dormite, in sacco, ministri Dei mei, id est veri Dei, quem ego propheta illius specialiter amo et colo. Illi enim Prophetæ Deum universorum nominant Deum suum, qui ei singulari uniuntur amore et reverentiali obsequio, qui dicere possunt : Deus cordis mei, et pars mea Deus in æternum. Quoniam interiit de domo Dei vestri, id est, cito in templo deficient, sacrificium et libatio : de quibus paulo ante jam dictum est, Periit sacrificium et libatio de domo Domini. Idcirco prædicta pœnitentiæ opera exercete, quatenus imminens vastitas tollatur a vobis.
paras.en: [[1:13|Gird yourselves|Accingite vos]] with sackcloth and haircloth [Denis's text adds these words, which the Vulgate lacks], [[1:13|and lament, O ye priests|et plangite, sacerdotes]]; [[1:13|howl, ye ministers of the altars|ululate, ministri altaris]]. He takes up the same sense in other words, to rouse his hearers more strongly. It belongs above all to priests to bewail their own sins and those of their subjects, and to reconcile God to the people, since they are mediators between God and the people, offering the prayers and victims of the people to God, and bringing back the grace of God to the people[[Heb 5:1||]]. And when the people's fault comes from the negligence of the priests, it is most fitting for the priests to weep for the reconciliation of the people: for the Lord too said to Moses that the sons of Aaron should bear the sins of the children of Israel[[Ex 28:38||]][[Num 18:1||]]. [[1:13|go in|Ingredimini]] to the temple, or to your own house, to pray; as the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:6|But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber|Tu autem quum oraveris, intra cubiculum tuum]], and [[Matt 6:6|pray to thy Father in secret|ora Patrem tuum in absconso]]; [[1:13|lie|cubate]], that is, sleep, [[1:13|in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God|in sacco, ministri Dei mei]], that is, of the true God, whom I, his prophet, love and worship in a special way. For those Prophets name the God of all things their own God who are united to him by a singular love and reverent service, who can say: [[Ps 72:26|the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever|Deus cordis mei, et pars mea Deus in æternum]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxii, 26: Ps. lxxii is meant]. For there [[1:13|is cut off from the house of your God|interiit de domo Dei vestri]] (that is, there will soon fail in the temple) [[1:13|sacrifice and libation|sacrificium et libatio]], of which it was said a little before: [[1:9|Sacrifice and libation is cut off from the house of the Lord|Periit sacrificium et libatio de domo Domini]]. Therefore perform the said works of penance, so that the threatened devastation may be taken from you.

paras.t: Solebant autem Judæi in veteri Testamento secundum præscriptam formam se humiliare, pœnitere, et Dominum invocare, ut patet in libris Regum, Paralipomenon, et Machabæorum. Quod autem hoc modo fecerunt sacerdotes ac ceteri, imminente captivitate Babylonica, patet in Threnis seu Lamentationibus Jeremiæ. Idem quoque refert eos fecisse Josephus instante captivitate Romana. Hinc per Jeremiam loquitur Dominus : Filia populi mei, accingere cilicio, et conspergere cinere; luctum unigeniti fac tibi, planctum amarum. Ad quod aliqui referunt illud Isaiæ : In die illa vocabit Dominus ad fletum, ad planctum, et ad cingulum sacci.
paras.en: Now the Jews in the Old Testament used to humble themselves, do penance and call upon the Lord according to a prescribed form, as is plain in the books of Kings, of Paralipomenon and of the Machabees. And that the priests and the rest did so when the Babylonian captivity was at hand is plain in the Threni or Lamentations of Jeremias. Josephus too relates that they did the same when the Roman captivity was at hand. Hence the Lord speaks through Jeremias: [[Jer 6:26|Gird thee with sackcloth, O daughter of my people, and sprinkle thee with ashes: make thee mourning as for an only son, a bitter lamentation|Filia populi mei, accingere cilicio, et conspergere cinere; luctum unigeniti fac tibi, planctum amarum]]. To this some refer that of Isaias: [[Is 22:12|the Lord, the God of hosts, in that day shall call to weeping, and to mourning|In die illa vocabit Dominus ad fletum, ad planctum]], [[Is 22:12|and to girding with sackcloth|et ad cingulum sacci]].

paras.t: Præterea adhuc Propheta præfigit sacerdotibus formam pœnitendi, et modum misericordiam implorandi. Sanctificate jejunium, id est, actum abstinentiæ in sanctitate peragite, bonis illum operibus adornate, et corda vestra ad devote jejunandum disponite. Non enim acceptum est Deo jejunium, nisi in caritate fiat et in observantia præceptorum. Hinc enim per Isaiam Dominus loquitur : Ecce in die jejunii vestri invenitur voluntas vestra. Numquid tale est jejunium quod ego elegi? Et Apostolus : Exerce te, inquit, ad pietatem; nam corporalis exercitatio ad modicum utilis est. Vocate cœtum, id est, cuneum populi convocate. Congregate senes, omnes habitatores terræ Judææ, de qua nunc sermo, in domum Dei vestri, quæ est domus orationis, videlicet in templum Jerusalem, in quo promisit se Deus preces orantium exauditurum. Præterea sacerdotum est, vulgum ac subditos adunare, et in modo pœnitendi et bene agendi instruere. Jubet quoque Propheta ut omnes generaliter convocentur atque in templo colligantur, quatenus oratio sit tanto exaudibilior, quanto a pluribus immolatur. Propter quod orat discipulos suos Apostolus orare pro se, ut ex multarum precibus personarum citius, quod petitur, obtineatur.
paras.en: Moreover the Prophet further sets before the priests the form of doing penance, and the way of imploring mercy. [[1:14|Sanctify ye a fast|Sanctificate jejunium]], that is, carry out the act of abstinence in holiness, adorn it with good works, and dispose your hearts to fast devoutly. For a fast is not acceptable to God unless it is done in charity and in the keeping of the commandments. Hence the Lord speaks through Isaias: [[Is 58:3|Behold in the day of your fast your own will is found|Ecce in die jejunii vestri invenitur voluntas vestra]]. [[Is 58:5|Is this such a fast as I have chosen|Numquid tale est jejunium quod ego elegi?]]? And the Apostle: [[1 Tim 4:7|exercise thyself|Exerce te]], he says, [[1 Tim 4:7|unto godliness|ad pietatem]]; [[1 Tim 4:8|For bodily exercise is profitable to little|nam corporalis exercitatio ad modicum utilis est]]. [[1:14|call an assembly|Vocate cœtum]], that is, call together the throng of the people. [[1:14|gather together the ancients, all the inhabitants of the land|Congregate senes, omnes habitatores terræ]] of Judea, of which he is now speaking, [[1:14|into the house of your God|in domum Dei vestri]], which is the house of prayer, namely into the temple of Jerusalem, in which God promised to hear the prayers of those who pray[[3 Kings 8:29||]]. Moreover it belongs to priests to gather the common people and their subjects together, and to instruct them in the manner of doing penance and of doing well. The Prophet also bids that all in general be called together and gathered in the temple, so that the prayer may be the more readily heard the more people offer it. For this reason the Apostle asks his disciples to pray for him, so that what is asked may be obtained the more quickly through the prayers of many persons[[2 Cor 1:11||]].

paras.t: Et clamate ad Dominum, dicentes : A, a, a, diei : id est, heu nobis propter mala diei ultionis, qui imminet nobis! Præcipit autem Propheta, ut ter dicant, A : vel propter majorem expressionem et faciliorem misericordiæ implorationem : unde in Jeremia habetur, Terra, terra, terra, audi verbum Domini; vel, quoniam sanctam Trinitatem offenderunt. Quidam dicit quod in Hebræo sit una dictio. Verumtamen pro eo quod Hieronymus transtulit ter A, Septuaginta transtulerunt, Heu mihi, heu mihi, heu mihi! Unde non videtur una dictio in Hebræo, nisi forte illa hanc tripartitam exclamationem significet. Quia prope est dies Domini, id est dies ultionis, in qua Dominus faciet vobis secundum suam voluntatem et æquitatem, debitas pœnas inferendo, sicut fecistis ei in diebus vestris, eum multipliciter secundum vestram voluntatem ac pravitatem inhonorando. Quamvis enim omne tempus omnisque dies sit Dei, illud tamen tempus dicitur specialiter ejus, in quo aliquid efficit novum, rarum aut speciale, sicut est dies vindictæ atque judicii. Dies quoque, nostri dicuntur, in quibus Deus permittit nos propriæ libertati, quando et operamur quæ volumus. Unde et Christus in Luca ait : Jerusalem, etc., et quidem in hac die tua, quæ ad pacem tibi. Et quasi vastitas a potente veniet : id est, sicut vastitas seu pressura, quam potens debiliori inducit, ineffugibiliter opprimit debiliorem, sic vindicta diei Domini irruet super vos, quod non effugietis.
paras.en: [[1:14|and cry ye to the Lord|Et clamate ad Dominum]], saying: [[1:15|Ah, ah, ah, for the day|A, a, a, diei]]: that is, woe to us for the evils of the day of vengeance that hangs over us! The Prophet bids them say *Ah* three times: either for greater expressiveness and an easier imploring of mercy (hence in Jeremias we have: [[Jer 22:29|O earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord|Terra, terra, terra, audi verbum Domini]]); or because they had offended the Holy Trinity. Someone says that in the Hebrew it is one word. Yet where Jerome translated *Ah* three times, the Seventy translated *Woe is me, woe is me, woe is me!* So it does not seem to be one word in the Hebrew, unless perhaps that word signifies this threefold exclamation. [[1:15|because the day of the Lord is at hand|Quia prope est dies Domini]], that is, the day of vengeance, in which the Lord will do to you according to his will and justice, inflicting due punishments, as you did to him in your days, dishonouring him in many ways according to your will and wickedness. For though every time and every day is God's, that time is called his in a special way in which he does something new, rare or special, such as the day of vengeance and judgement. And those days are called ours in which God leaves us to our own freedom, when we also do what we will. Hence Christ too says in Luke: Jerusalem, etc., [[Luke 19:42|and that in this thy day, the things that are to thy peace|et quidem in hac die tua, quæ ad pacem tibi]]. [[1:15|and it shall come like destruction from the mighty|Et quasi vastitas a potente veniet]]: that is, as the devastation or oppression that a powerful man brings on a weaker crushes the weaker inescapably, so the vengeance of the day of the Lord will rush upon you, so that you will not escape it.

paras.t: Numquid non coram oculis vestris, id est in vestra præsentia seu conspectu, alimenta defecerunt, id est, statim deficient? Deficiet quoque de domo Dei vestri, id est de templo, lætitia cordis et exsultatio corporis : quoniam immolatione hostiarum cessante, sacerdotes in templo non habuerunt materiam gloriandi, sed lamentandi. Quæ omnia tunc impleta noscuntur, quando Assyrii et Chaldæi ingressi ac demoliti sunt terram Judææ.
paras.en: [[1:16|Is not|Numquid non]] [[1:16|before your eyes|coram oculis vestris]], that is, in your presence or sight, [[1:16|your food cut off|alimenta defecerunt]] [the edition notes another reading, *perierunt*, have perished, as in the Vulgate], that is, will it not straightway fail? There will fail too [[1:16|from the house of our God|de domo Dei vestri]] [Denis reads *your God*], that is, from the temple, [[1:16|joy and gladness|lætitia cordis et exsultatio corporis]] [Denis reads *joy of heart and gladness of body*]: since, when the offering of victims ceased, the priests in the temple had no matter for glorying, but for lamenting. All these things are known to have been fulfilled when the Assyrians and Chaldeans came in and laid waste the land of Judea[[4 Kings 17:1||]][[4 Kings 25:1||]].

paras.t: Computruerunt jumenta in stercore suo. Hoc ad litteram accipi potest, quod jumenta quæ in stabulis non habebant stramenta propter bladorum defectum, jacuerunt, computrueruntque in suis fæcibus atque stercoribus. Vel sensus est, quod jumenta, id est homines carnales, gulosi, luxuriosi, in sordibus vitiorum suorum resoluti atque consumpti sunt, juxta illud Psalmi: Putruerunt et corruptæ sunt cicatrices meæ; et iterum, Homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit, comparatus est jumentis insipientibus. Demolita, id est ab hostibus destructa sunt horrea, dissipatæ sunt apothecæ, id est repositoria victualium, cum his quæ continebantur in eis, quoniam confusum, id est sublatum ex horreis, est triticum.
paras.en: [[1:17|The beasts have rotted in their dung|Computruerunt jumenta in stercore suo]]. This can be taken literally: that the beasts, which had no litter in the stalls for lack of grain, lay down and rotted in their filth and dung. Or the sense is that the beasts, that is, carnal, gluttonous and lustful men, were dissolved and consumed in the filth of their vices, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 37:6|My sores are putrefied and corrupted|Putruerunt et corruptæ sunt cicatrices meæ]]; and again, [[Ps 48:13|man when he was in honour did not understand; he is compared to senseless beasts|Homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit, comparatus est jumentis insipientibus]]. [[1:17|the barns are destroyed|Demolita]], that is, destroyed by the enemies; [[1:17|the storehouses are broken down|dissipatæ sunt apothecæ]], that is, the storerooms of victuals, with what was contained in them; [[1:17|because the corn is confounded|quoniam confusum]], that is, taken out of the barns.

paras.t: Quid ingemuit animal? id est, cur bestiæ præ inedia famis clamaverunt, aut singultum quemdam fecerunt? et quid mugierunt greges armenti? Et respondet: Quia non est pascua eis, id est alimonia, consumptis virentibus terræ et fructibus. Translatio Septuaginta interpretum sic habet: Fleverunt armenta boum. Idcirco Hieronymus istud de hominibus accipit, qui propter simplicitatem aut stoliditatem, bestialemve conversationem, nominibus bestiarum exprimuntur. Sed et greges ovium disperierunt: hostes enim rapuerunt oves et comederunt. Vel præ fame defecerunt. Vel deficiente pane, Judæi pecora sua manducare compulsi sunt.
paras.en: [[1:18|Why did the beasts groan|Quid ingemuit animal]]? that is, why did the beasts cry out for want of food, or make a kind of sobbing? [[1:18|why did the herds of cattle low|et quid mugierunt greges armenti]]? And he answers: [[1:18|because there is no pasture for them|Quia non est pascua eis]], that is, no nourishment, the green things and fruits of the earth having been consumed. The translation of the Seventy has: *The herds of oxen have wept*. Therefore Jerome takes this of men who, because of their simplicity or dullness, or their beastlike way of life, are expressed by the names of beasts. [[1:18|yea, and the flocks of sheep are perished|Sed et greges ovium disperierunt]]: for the enemies carried off the sheep and ate them. Or they perished from hunger. Or, when bread failed, the Jews were forced to eat their own flocks.

paras.t: Ad te, Domine, clamabo, orando pro populo tuo, quia ignis comedit speciosa deserti, id est, eruca, locusta, bruchus, ventusque urens blada rubiginans, devoraverunt seu arida fecerunt plana loca camporum, prata et quaslibet terras virentes, quæ jumentis pascua præbuerunt, et flamma succendit omnia ligna regionis, id est arbores Judææ. Solet autem per ignem quælibet magna tribulatio vel persecutio gravissima designari. Sed et Chaldæi utique igne materiali incenderunt speciosa quæ in desertis Judææ steterunt, et arbores regionis hujus combusserunt.
paras.en: [[1:19|To thee, O Lord, will I cry|Ad te, Domine, clamabo]], praying for thy people, [[1:19|because fire hath devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness|quia ignis comedit speciosa deserti]]: that is, the palmerworm, locust, bruchus, and the burning wind that blights the grain with mildew, have devoured or made dry the level stretches of the plains, the meadows and all green lands, which gave pasture to the beasts; [[1:19|and the flame hath burnt all the trees of the country|et flamma succendit omnia ligna regionis]], that is, the trees of Judea. Now by fire any great tribulation or most grievous persecution is commonly signified. But the Chaldeans too certainly burned with material fire the beautiful things that stood in the wildernesses of Judea, and burned up the trees of this country.

paras.t: Sed et bestiæ agri, id est indomitæ vel silvestres, quasi area sitiens imbrem, id est humore indigens et aquam desiderans, suspexerunt ad te: non quod bestiæ Deum agnoscant, aut invocent proprie; sed metaphorice dicuntur ad Deum adspicere et clamare, in quantum cibum naturaliter optant ac potum, quæ non habent nisi per providentiam Dei. Unde in Evangelio dicitur, quod Pater cœlestis pascit ea; et in Psalmo, Qui dat jumentis escam ipsorum, et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum; in Job quoque, Quis præparat corvo escam, quando pulli ejus clamant ad Deum, vagientes eo quod non habent cibos? Rursusque in Psalmo: Omnia a te exspectant ut des illis escam in tempore; et, Oculi omnium in te sperant, Domine. Quoniam exsiccati sunt fontes aquarum, a multitudine hostium, quorum equi et servi aquas fontium consumpserunt, vel, a vehementi flatu venti urentis, qui siccitatem inducit; et ignis devoravit speciosa deserti, secundum sensum jam tactum: sicque bestiæ silvestres nec cibum habuerunt, nec potum.
paras.en: [[1:20|Yea, and the beasts of the field|Sed et bestiæ agri]], that is, the untamed or wild ones, [[1:20|as a garden bed that thirsteth after rain|quasi area sitiens imbrem]] [*area*, properly a threshing floor], that is, lacking moisture and longing for water, [[1:20|have looked up to thee|suspexerunt ad te]]: not that beasts know God or call upon him in the proper sense; but they are said metaphorically to look up and cry to God in so far as they naturally long for food and drink, which they have only through the providence of God. Hence it is said in the Gospel that [[Matt 6:26|your heavenly Father feedeth them|Pater cœlestis pascit ea]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 146:9|Who giveth to beasts their food: and to the young ravens that call upon him|Qui dat jumentis escam ipsorum, et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum]]; in Job too: [[Job 38:41|Who provideth food for the raven, when her young ones cry to God, wandering about, because they have no meat?|Quis præparat corvo escam, quando pulli ejus clamant ad Deum, vagientes eo quod non habent cibos?]] And again in the Psalm: [[Ps 103:27|All expect of thee that thou give them food in season|Omnia a te exspectant ut des illis escam in tempore]]; and: [[Ps 144:15|The eyes of all hope in thee, O Lord|Oculi omnium in te sperant, Domine]]. [[1:20|for the springs of waters are dried up|Quoniam exsiccati sunt fontes aquarum]]: by the multitude of the enemies, whose horses and servants used up the waters of the springs; or by the violent blast of the burning wind, which brings drought; [[1:20|and fire hath devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness|et ignis devoravit speciosa deserti]], in the sense already touched on: and so the wild beasts had neither food nor drink.

1.title: Elucidatio tropologica [ejusdem capituli primi].
1.title_en: Tropological explanation of the same first chapter.

paras.t: Joel interpretatur aperiens, Phatuel latitudo. Qui igitur bonum virtutis viriliter incipit, filius fit latitudinis, id est gratiæ amplioris et caritatis ardentis, ut dicere queat cum Paulo, Cor nostrum dilatatum est; et cum Psalmista, Et ambulabam in latitudine, quia mandata tua exquisivi. Quid enim latius caritate, quæ omnia ambit, atque ad hostes extenditur, et universis, quæ habet, communicat? Ad talem quoque fit verbum Dei, quoniam Spiritus Sanctus inspirat ei pertinentia ad salutem, sicut ait Joannes, Unctio docet vos de omnibus: ita ut valeat dicere, Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus. Quum enim incipit rationalis creatura quod bonum est, mox adest Spiritus, qui adjuvat infirmitatem nostram. Ideoque cum plena divinæ subventionis fiducia viriliter est inchoandum, ut humiliter magnanimiterque dicamus: Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat; itemque: Dominus dabit benignitatem, et terra nostra dabit fructum suum. Quidam vero propriam imbecillitatem, non divinæ pietatis virtutem, pensantes, nimis pusillanimes sunt, non audentes ad aratrum ponere manum, divinæ bonitatis superliberalissimæ munificentiæ derogantes.
paras.en: Joel is interpreted *opening*, Phatuel *breadth*. He therefore who manfully begins the good of virtue becomes a son of breadth, that is, of more abundant grace and of burning charity, so that he can say with Paul, [[2 Cor 6:11|our heart is enlarged|Cor nostrum dilatatum est]]; and with the Psalmist, [[Ps 118:45|And I walked at large: because I have sought after thy commandments|Et ambulabam in latitudine, quia mandata tua exquisivi]]. For what is broader than charity, which embraces all things, reaches out even to enemies, and shares with all men whatever it has? To such a one also the word of God comes, since the Holy Spirit breathes into him the things that pertain to salvation, as John says, The [[1 John 2:27|unction teacheth you of all things|Unctio docet vos de omnibus]]: so that he is able to say, [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me|Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]]. For as soon as a rational creature begins what is good, the Spirit is at hand, who [[Rom 8:26|helpeth our infirmity|adjuvat infirmitatem nostram]]. And therefore we must begin manfully, with full confidence in God's help, so as to say humbly and magnanimously: [[Phil 4:13|I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me|Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat]]; and again: [[Ps 84:13|the Lord will give goodness: and our earth shall yield her fruit|Dominus dabit benignitatem, et terra nostra dabit fructum suum]]. But some, weighing their own weakness and not the power of God's loving-kindness, are too faint-hearted, not daring to put their hand to the plough[[Luke 9:62||]], and so detracting from the most superabundantly liberal bounty of the divine goodness.

paras.t: Audite hoc, senes; et auribus percipite, omnes habitatores terræ: id est, spiritualem intelligentiam propheticorum verborum Joelis, universi Christiani senes juvenesque, attendite.
paras.en: [[1:2|Hear this, ye old men, and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land|Audite hoc, senes; et auribus percipite, omnes habitatores terræ]]: that is, all ye Christians, old and young, attend to the spiritual understanding of the prophetic words of Joel.

paras.t: Residuum erucæ comedit locusta, etc. Per quatuor ista intelligo quatuor vitia, quatuor virtutibus cardinalibus contraria, quæ sunt: Intemperantia, timiditas, injustitia, et indiscretio. — Intemperantia autem, bona animæ magna ex parte devastat et ejicit, quoniam nisi vitia gulæ et luxuriæ exstirpentur, non fit homo spiritualium capax donorum, Domino contestante: Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est. Et Apostolus ad Romanos: Qui (inquit) in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt. Ideo Petrus hortatur a carnalibus desideriis, quæ militant adversus animam, abstinere. Hinc et Isaias disseruit: Quem docebit Dominus scientiam, et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere, eos videlicet, qui vitia intemperantiæ detestantur.
paras.en: [[1:4|That which the palmerworm hath left, the locust hath eaten|Residuum erucæ comedit locusta]], etc. By these four I understand four vices, contrary to the four cardinal virtues, namely: intemperance, timidity, injustice and indiscretion [that is, want of discretion, the right judgement of measure that belongs to prudence]. Intemperance, then, lays waste and casts out the goods of the soul in great part, since unless the vices of gluttony and lust are rooted out, a man does not become capable of spiritual gifts, as the Lord testifies: [[Gen 6:3|My spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh|Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est]]. And the Apostle to the Romans: [[Rom 8:8|they who|Qui]] (he says) [[Rom 8:8|are in the flesh cannot please God|in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt]]. Therefore Peter exhorts us to abstain [[1 Pet 2:11|from carnal desires which war against the soul|a carnalibus desideriis, quæ militant adversus animam]]. Hence Isaias too declared: [[Is 28:9|Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand the hearing? them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts|Quem docebit Dominus scientiam, et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere]]: those, namely, who detest the vices of intemperance.

paras.t: Denique hoc tam manifesto detestandoque vitio non vincuntur, sed timiditate, veræ fortitudini (quæ magnanimiter aggreditur fortia) repugnante, inordinate timentes ubi non est timor, et propriæ pelli timentes, malunt incidere mala culpæ et Dei offensam, quam mala pœnæ hominumque indignationem. Quocontra ait Salvator: Nolite timere eos qui occidunt corpus; et Isaias: Quis tu, ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis, qui quasi fœnum arescit? Hac vili timiditate carebat, qui dicebat: Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me; et: Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea: quem timebo? Porro, teste Scriptura, qui timet Dominum, nihil trepidabit. His itaque sacris testimoniis increpantur vilia corda quorumdam, hominum magis quam Deum timentium: qui in præsentia superiorum suorum quamdam confingunt ac induunt gravitatem, sed illis abeuntibus, ad consuetas redeunt culpas, negligentias, et excessus. Hi non agunt bonum amore boni, sed timore mali: in quibus residuum erucæ edit locusta. De qua plaga eripitur, qui illud Proverbiorum implet: Fili, honora Dominum, et valebis; præter eum vero ne timueris alienum. — juxta LXX.
paras.en: Many [the print has *Denique*, "finally", with *Plerique*, "many", given beside it as the reading] are not overcome by this so manifest and detestable vice, but by timidity, which is opposed to true fortitude (which magnanimously takes on hard things): fearing inordinately [[Ps 13:5|where there was no fear|ubi non est timor]], and fearing for their own skin, they would rather fall into the evils of guilt and the offence of God than into the evils of punishment and the indignation of men. Against this the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:28|fear ye not them that kill the body|Nolite timere eos qui occidunt corpus]]; and Isaias: [[Is 51:12|who art thou, that thou shouldst be afraid of a mortal man, and of the son of man, who shall wither away like grass?|Quis tu, ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis, qui quasi fœnum arescit?]] He was free of this base timidity who said: [[Ps 3:7|I will not fear thousands of the people surrounding me|Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me]]; and: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?|Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea: quem timebo?]] Moreover, as Scripture testifies, [[Ecclus 34:16|He that feareth the Lord shall tremble at nothing|qui timet Dominum, nihil trepidabit]]. By these sacred testimonies, then, are rebuked the base hearts of certain men who fear men more than God: who in the presence of their superiors put on and feign a certain gravity, but when these have gone away return to their accustomed faults, negligences and excesses. These do not do good for love of the good, but for fear of evil: in them [[1:4|That which the palmerworm hath left, the locust hath eaten|residuum erucæ edit locusta]]. From this plague he is delivered who fulfils that saying of Proverbs: Son, honour the Lord, and thou shalt be strong; but besides him fear no stranger[[Prov 7:1||]]: according to the Seventy. [In the Clementine Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims these words end Prov 7:1, "Son, honour the Lord, and thou shalt be strong: and beside him fear no stranger"; the text of the verse in the app breaks off at "Son,".]

paras.t: Qui autem nec intemperantia nec timiditate prædicta dejiciuntur, frequenter peccato injustitiæ superantur, non reddendo singulis quæ sua sunt, neque, juxta principis Apostolorum doctrinam, unusquisque, sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, tanquam boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei. In his residuum locustæ comedit bruchus. — Alii prædictis vitiis reluctantes, per indiscretionem labuntur: quorum non rationabile est obsequium, qui quoniam plus faciunt quam possunt, dispereunt. In quibus ærugo consumit quod inerat, inesseve poterat animæ. — Insuper, per quatuor plagas has intelligi possunt quatuor tentationes principales, vel quatuor primi ac maximi persecutores Ecclesiæ, seu quatuor principaliores hæresiarchæ, qui infinitas animas spiritualiter jugulaverunt.
paras.en: But those who are not cast down by intemperance or by the timidity just described are frequently overcome by the sin of injustice, not rendering to each what is his, nor, according to the teaching of the prince of the Apostles, [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another: as good stewards of the manifold grace of God|unusquisque, sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, tanquam boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei]]. In these [[1:4|that which the locust hath left, the bruchus hath eaten|residuum locustæ comedit bruchus]]. Others, struggling against the vices already named, fall through indiscretion: their service is not reasonable[[Rom 12:1||]], and because they do more than they can, they perish[[Jer 48:36||]]. In these the rust [Denis writes *ærugo*, rust, for the *rubigo*, mildew, of the verse] consumes what was in the soul, or could have been in it. Moreover, by these four plagues can be understood the four principal temptations, or the four first and greatest persecutors of the Church, or the four chief heresiarchs, who spiritually slaughtered countless souls.

paras.t: Expergiscimini, ebrii, et flete. Hoc est quod ait Apostolus: Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis; itemque Salvator, Vigilate, quia nescitis diem neque horam. Denique impii ebrii, sunt omnes qui carnalibus delectationibus, mundanis vanitatibus, aut ceteris inordinatis passionum affectionibus sic resolvuntur et vacant, quod judicium rationis non advertunt, nec Deo neque Ecclesiæ parent, sed in proprii ambulant cordis pravitate. Unde in Jeremia habetur: Usquequo deliciis dissolveris, filia vaga? Et ululate, omnes qui bibitis vinum in dulcedine. De quibus scriptum est apud Isaiam: Væ qui consurgitis mane ad ebrietatem sectandam, et potandum usque ad vesperam; et in Proverbiis scriptum est, Væ his qui commorantur in vino, et student calicibus epotandis. Quam multi modo sunt tales, qui et corpus suum et animam perimunt! Vinum enim moderate sumptum, sanitas est corporis et animæ; sed superflue sumptum, mordet ut coluber. Quoniam periit ab ore vestro: id est, omnis carnalis voluptas cito vertetur vobis in mœrorem æternalemque pœnam, nisi pœnitentiam veram egeritis, quemadmodum factum est diviti qui epulabatur quotidie splendide. Vidua nempe in deliciis vivens, secundum Apostolum, vivens mortua est. Et apud Lucam comminatus est Christus: Væ vobis qui saturati estis, quia esuritis. Propterea in Ecclesiastico asseritur: Si præstiteris animæ tuæ concupiscentias ejus, facient te in gaudium inimicis tuis. Momentaneum est quod nunc delectat, æternum vero quod cruciat.
paras.en: [[1:5|Awake, ye that are drunk, and weep|Expergiscimini, ebrii, et flete]]. This is what the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead|Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis]]; and the Saviour likewise, [[Matt 25:13|Watch ye therefore, because you know not the day nor the hour|Vigilate, quia nescitis diem neque horam]]. The wicked drunkards, then, are all who are so loosened by and given up to carnal delights, worldly vanities, or the other inordinate affections of the passions, that they pay no heed to the judgement of reason and obey neither God nor the Church, but walk in the perversity of their own heart. Hence it is said in Jeremias: [[Jer 31:22|How long wilt thou be dissolute in deliciousness, O wandering daughter?|Usquequo deliciis dissolveris, filia vaga?]] [[1:5|and mourn all ye that take delight in drinking sweet wine|Et ululate, omnes qui bibitis vinum in dulcedine]]. Of these it is written in Isaias: [[Is 5:11|Woe to you that rise up early in the morning to follow drunkenness, and to drink in the evening|Væ qui consurgitis mane ad ebrietatem sectandam, et potandum usque ad vesperam]]; and in Proverbs it is written, Woe[[Prov 23:29||]] to these: [[Prov 23:30|they that pass their time in wine, and study to drink off their cups|qui commorantur in vino, et student calicibus epotandis]]. How many there are now of this kind, who destroy both their body and their soul! For wine taken in moderation is health of body and soul[[Ecclus 31:37||]]; but taken to excess, [[Prov 23:32|it will bite like a snake|mordet ut coluber]]. [[1:5|for it is cut off from your mouth|Quoniam periit ab ore vestro]]: that is, every carnal pleasure will soon be turned for you into grief and eternal punishment, unless you do true penance, as befell the rich man who [[Luke 16:19|feasted sumptuously every day|epulabatur quotidie splendide]][[Luke 16:22||]]. For the widow living in pleasures, according to the Apostle, [[1 Tim 5:6|is dead while she is living|vivens mortua est]]. And in Luke Christ threatened: [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that are filled: for you shall hunger|Væ vobis qui saturati estis, quia esuritis]]. Therefore it is declared in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 18:31|If thou give to thy soul her desires, she will make thee a joy to thy enemies|Si præstiteris animæ tuæ concupiscentias ejus, facient te in gaudium inimicis tuis]]. What delights now is momentary; what torments is eternal.

paras.t: Præterea hoc loco ait Hieronymus: Nulla res ita inebriat, ut animi perturbatio. Est tristitia quæ ducit ad mortem: hæc abominanda ebrietas est. Est ira quæ justitiam Dei non operatur, et furori proxima mentis impotem facit, in tantum ut labia tremant, dentes concrepent, vultus pallore mutetur. Quid referam de gaudio et voluptate, et maxime de amore qui excæcat cordis oculos, et nihil aliud amantem, nisi quod amat, cogitare permittit? Annon est dicenda ebrietas, quum propter vile scortum, animæ libertas in serviles blanditias inclinatur?
paras.en: Further, Jerome says on this place: Nothing makes drunk like the disturbance of the mind. There is a sorrow that leads to death: this is an abominable drunkenness. There is an anger that [[Jas 1:20|worketh not the justice of God|justitiam Dei non operatur]], and, being next to fury, makes a man not master of his mind, so that his lips tremble, his teeth chatter, and his face changes with pallor. What shall I say of joy and pleasure, and above all of love, which blinds the eyes of the heart and lets the lover think of nothing but what he loves? Must it not be called drunkenness when, for the sake of a vile harlot, the freedom of the soul is bent down to servile flatteries?

paras.t: Gens enim ascendet super terram meam, fortis et innumerabilis: id est, visibiles ac invisibiles hostes (nam et de diabolo dictum est, Inimicus homo hoc fecit), invaserunt militantem Ecclesiam seu animam christianam devotam, ut eam a Deo avertant. Mundus enim et dæmon indesinenter tentant electos, qui in medio ambulant laqueorum, et propter justitiam plurima patiuntur adversa, quemadmodum legitur: Omnes qui pie volunt vivere in Christo, persecutionem patientur. Quoniam ergo tot hostibus atque periculis circumvallatur Ecclesia, prælati qui delectationibus vacant et negligentia dissolvuntur, jubentur evigilare a somno ignaviæ, flere et ululare, quatenus gregi suo debitam impendant custodiam, Deumque pro illius salute lacrimabiliter invocent.
paras.en: [[1:6|For a nation come up upon my land, strong, and without number|Gens enim ascendet super terram meam, fortis et innumerabilis]] [Denis reads *ascendet*, "shall come up"]: that is, visible and invisible enemies (for of the devil too it is said, [[Matt 13:28|An enemy hath done this|Inimicus homo hoc fecit]]) have invaded the Church militant, or the devout Christian soul, to turn it away from God. For the world and the demon tempt the elect unceasingly, who walk in the midst of snares and suffer very many adversities for justice' sake, as we read: [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ|Omnes qui pie volunt vivere in Christo]] [[2 Tim 3:12|shall suffer persecution|persecutionem patientur]]. Since, then, the Church is hemmed in by so many enemies and dangers, the prelates who give themselves to pleasures and are slack with negligence are commanded to awake from the sleep of sloth, to weep and to howl, so that they may give their flock the watch they owe it, and call upon God with tears for its salvation.

paras.t: Dentes ejus, ut dentes leonis. De quo Petrus: Adversarius, inquit, vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret. Quid enim crudelius his qui animas conantur occidere, et ab æterno infinitoque bono eas avertere, sicque in sempiterna inferni tormenta pertrahere?
paras.en: [[1:6|his teeth are like the teeth of a lion|Dentes ejus, ut dentes leonis]]. Of whom Peter says: [[1 Pet 5:8|your adversary|Adversarius]], he says, [[1 Pet 5:8|the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour|vester diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret]]. For what is more cruel than those who strive to kill souls, to turn them away from the eternal and infinite good, and so to drag them into the everlasting torments of hell?

paras.t: Posuit vineam meam in desertum, id est, Ecclesiam, quoad aliquam ejus partem, spiritualibus bonis destituit, inducendo fideles ad consensum peccati, quo a Deo deseritur; et ficum meam, id est animam quæ dulcissimis bonis ac fructibus Spiritus Sancti abundavit, decorticavit, id est, a pristinis bonis minoravit, sive abscidit. Tales sunt, qui quum cœperint spiritu, carne consummantur. Istud Christus præcipue dicit de claustralibus non observantibus regulam suam, qui a statu perfectionis ad sæcularia vitia devolvuntur.
paras.en: [[1:7|He hath laid my vineyard waste|Posuit vineam meam in desertum]], that is, he has stripped the Church, as to some part of it, of spiritual goods, by leading the faithful to consent to sin, through which it is forsaken by God; [[1:7|and hath pilled off the bark of my fig tree|et ficum meam decorticavit]], that is, the soul that abounded in the sweetest goods and fruits of the Holy Spirit, he has *pilled*, that is, diminished it in its former goods, or cut them off. Such are they who, having begun in the spirit, are finished in the flesh[[Gal 3:3||]]. Christ says this especially of cloistered religious who do not keep their rule, who sink down from the state of perfection into worldly vices.

paras.t: Plange quasi virgo accincta sacco super virum pubertatis suæ.
